header_desc_1: DarkMoon Engine is a graphics engine built from scratch in C++23 and OpenGL. It started as the backbone for Two Wonders, built to handle the project's technical needs without falling apart under complex scenes.
header_desc_2: This new version is focused exclusively on 2D, with a cleaner and more modular architecture than its predecessor. The original code was refactored top to bottom to make everything easier to understand, extend, and maintain.
header_ecs: Entity Component System built on a custom SlotMap and compile-time type metaprogramming. Header-only, no dynamic allocations, and designed for you to instantiate with your own types.
whatis_desc: ECS is a pattern that separates data (components) from logic (systems), using lightweight IDs (entities) to connect them.
whatis_core_entity: Entity: a numeric ID with a bitmask that tracks which components and tags it owns. No data of its own.
whatis_core_component: Component: a plain data struct (e.g. PhysicsComponent, RenderComponent). No logic, no weird inheritance.
whatis_core_tag: Tag: an empty struct that acts as a boolean flag (e.g. TagPlayer, TagEnemy). Takes up nothing in the SlotMap.
whatis_core_system: System: a struct with an update(EM&, ...) method that loops over entities and does things with their components.
whatis_core_em: Entity Manager: the core. Owns all entities and their component storage. You instantiate it with your own types.
whatis_design_headeronly: Header-only, all of it. Everything lives in .hpp files because it's template-based, and that makes it much easier to drop into any project.
whatis_design_slotmap: Each component type gets its own SlotMap, giving O(1) access and cache-friendly iteration.
whatis_design_bitmask: Bitmasks are resolved at compile time via MP::cmp_tag_traits. No type lookups at runtime.
whatis_design_limits: Defaults are 200 entities and 350 slots per SlotMap. Both are template parameters, so you can change them.
whatis_design_types: You define CMPList and TAGList in types.hpp. The engine doesn't assume anything about your types.
architecture_desc: DarkMoon resolves everything at compile time. You define which components and tags exist, and the engine builds on top of that with no runtime overhead.
architecture_dataflow_desc: Everything starts from types.hpp. From there you instantiate the EntityManager and you're good to go create entities, add components, run queries, and iterate with lambdas.
typeshpp_desc: types.hpp is the file you have to create and edit when you add components or tags. This is where you instantiate the EntityManager with your concrete types.
architecture_types_reminder: Don't forget to add every new component or tag to CMPList / TAGList in types.hpp. If you skip this, the EntityManager won't know they exist.
components_desc: Components are plain data structs. No logic, no weird methods, just data.
components_list_1: They must be default-constructible that's a SlotMap requirement.
components_list_2: Keep them small and focused. One component, one thing.
components_list_3: They can hold heap data via std::unique_ptr, but watch out for move semantics when the SlotMap reorganizes storage.
tags_desc: Tags are empty structs that work as boolean flags. They only take up a single bit in the entity's bitmask and don't allocate any slot in the SlotMap.
systems_desc: Systems are structs with an update() method that takes the EM by reference. They use forEach to iterate only the entities they care about.
systems_callout: Declare SYSCMPs and SYSTAGs as aliases inside the struct. It makes the system self-documenting and future-you will be grateful.
entities_api_desc: How to create, look up, and destroy entities.
api_newEntity: Creates a new entity and returns a reference to it. Hits an assert if you reach MAX_ENTITIES (200).
api_destroyEntityByID: Destroys the entity with that ID and all its components. Uses swap-with-last internally so it's O(1).
api_destroyEntities: Batch-destroys a set of entities. The set must be sorted in descending order (std::greater) to avoid index invalidation mid-removal.
api_destroyAll: Wipes everything entities and component storages. Clean slate.
api_getEntityByID: Returns a pointer to the entity with that ID, or nullptr if it doesn't exist. Linear search, don't call this every frame.
api_getEntities: Returns a span over all currently alive entities. Safe to iterate as long as you're not destroying entities in the middle of it.
api_aliveCount: How many entities are alive right now.
api_freeEntities: How many more entities you can create before hitting MAX_ENTITIES.
api_entity_getID: The unique ID of this entity. Assigned sequentially and never reused within a session.
api_entity_hasComponent: Returns true if the entity owns a component of type T. Bitmask check: O(1).
api_entity_hasTag: Returns true if the entity has that tag. Bitmask check: O(1).
components_api_desc: Adding, accessing, and removing components and tags on entities.
api_addComponent: Adds a component of type T to entity e, forwarding args to its constructor. If the entity already has that component, returns the existing one without creating a new one.
api_getComponent: Returns a reference to the component of type T on entity e. Asserts if the entity does not have that component, always check with hasComponent first if unsure.
api_destroyComponent: Removes the component of type T from entity e and frees its slot in the SlotMap. No-op if the entity does not have that component.
api_addTag: Sets the tag bit for type T on entity e. Tags have no storage, only the bitmask bit is flipped.
api_destroyTag: Clears the tag bit for type T on entity e.
section_iteration_desc: Iterating entities that match a set of required components and tags.
api_forEach: Calls func(Entity&, CMP&...) for every alive entity that has all components in CMPs and all tags in TAGs. The component references are passed as arguments to the lambda in the same order as CMPs.
api_forEachAny: Calls func(Entity&) for every entity that has any component in CMPs or any tag in TAGs. No component references are passed use getComponent inside the lambda.
slotmap_desc: Each component type gets its own Slotmap<T, Capacity> instance inside the EntityManager. The SlotMap provides O(1) insert, erase, and lookup while keeping all live data packed contiguously in memory — critical for cache performance during forEach iteration.
slotmap_param_capacity: Maximum number of elements. Fixed at compile-time; set via MAX_ENTITIES in types.hpp.
slotmap_param_indext: Integer type used for indices and generations. Use uint16_t to reduce memory on small worlds.
slotmap_arrays_desc: Three fixed-size arrays work together to provide stable keys over a packed data buffer.
slotmap_key_desc: A key_type is a small POD pair returned by push_back. The generation field makes stale-key detection free — no extra bookkeeping required at the call site.
slotmap_api_push_move: Insert by move. Throws std::runtime_error if full.
slotmap_api_push_copy: Insert by copy (delegates to move overload).
slotmap_api_access: Unchecked access. Asserts validity in debug builds.
slotmap_api_erase: Remove element. Returns false if key is already invalid.
slotmap_api_isvalid: Check whether a key still refers to a live element.
slotmap_api_clear: Reset all slots and reinitialise the freelist.
slotmap_api_iter: Raw iterators over the packed data range [0, size).
slotmap_swappop_desc: When an element is erased and it is not the last one in m_data, the last element is moved into the freed slot. Three pointer fixups keep everything consistent:
slotmap_swappop_after: The slot for B is returned to the freelist and its generation is bumped. Any stored key_type for B now fails is_valid() because m_indices[b].gen != key.gen.
slotmap_callout: The EntityManager stores one Slotmap<CMP, MAX_ENTITIES> per component type in a std::tuple. Access is via std::get<Index>(m_slotmaps), where the index is resolved at compile-time through MP::IndexOf.
metaprog_desc: All compile-time logic lives in the MP:: namespace inside meta_program.hpp. It is a self-contained, zero-dependency header that reimplements the type-traits machinery needed by EntityManager without relying on <type_traits>. Every facility is consteval or resolved at compile-time — no runtime cost.
metaprog_foundational_desc: The header starts by defining its own Boolean and value constants, keeping the namespace self-contained.
metaprog_nth_title: nth_type — index into a parameter pack
metaprog_nth_desc: Extracts the N-th type from a variadic pack via recursive specialisation. Used internally by TypeList and cmp_tag_traits.
metaprog_pos_desc: Walks the pack at compile-time and returns the zero-based index of T. Triggers a static assert if T is not present.
metaprog_ift_desc: Selects between two types based on a boolean condition. Equivalent to std::conditional. Used by smallest_type to pick the narrowest integer that fits the bitmask.
metaprog_typelist_desc: The main user-facing type. A variadic struct with no data members — pure compile-time information. Exposes three consteval member functions.
metaprog_smallest_desc: Given a TypeList, selects the narrowest unsigned integer that can hold one bit per type. This is the mask_type used by every entity to store its component/tag bitmask.
metaprog_smallest_callout: The maximum combined total of components + tags is 64, enforced by a static_assert inside cmp_tag_traits. Exceeding this limit is a compile error.
metaprog_traits_desc: The central metaprogramming type consumed by EntityManager. Given the full merged TypeList of all components and tags, it exposes the mask_type and the consteval mask() function used to build query masks at compile-time.
metaprog_traits_callout: An empty TypeList<> specialisation of cmp_tag_traits is provided so that passing an empty component or tag list to forEach always compiles cleanly and produces a mask of 0 (matches everything).
metaprog_transformers_desc: Two additional helpers allow reusing a TypeList with different wrappers, used internally to build the std::tuple of SlotMaps.
metaprog_foreachtuple_desc: A runtime helper that calls a lambda on every element of a std::tuple, iterating by index via template recursion. Used by EntityManager to reset all SlotMaps on destroyAll() and to build bitmask queries that touch each component storage in turn.
metaprog_ref_constant: Holds a single compile-time value V of type T.
metaprog_ref_nth: Extracts the N-th type from a parameter pack.
metaprog_ref_smallest: Narrowest uintN_t that fits one bit per type in TL.
metaprog_ref_foreachtuple: Calls f(element) for every element of a std::tuple.
iteration_callout: Do not call destroyEntityByID() or destroyEntities() from inside a forEach lambda. Collect IDs into a deathSet during iteration and destroy them after the loop.
example1_desc: Create an entity, add a component, retrieve it, and query its existence. This is the minimal lifecycle every ECS interaction is built on: newEntity → addComponent → getComponent → hasComponent.
example2_desc: One entity can carry any subset of the registered components. Shows how to compose a player (Position + Velocity + Health), a static enemy (Position + Health), and a pickup (Position only), then how forEach filters strictly by intersection — only entities that own every requested component are visited.
example3_desc: Tags are empty structs that consume a single bitmask bit and no SlotMap slot. This example uses TagPlayer, TagEnemy, and TagInvincible to categorize entities and gate damage logic — including adding and removing TagInvincible at runtime to simulate a power-up effect.
example4_desc: Three systems (MovementSystem, BoundsSystem, CombatSystem) each declare their own SYSCMPs / SYSTAGs and expose a single update(EM&) method. The main loop owns only the EntityManager and calls the systems in order every frame, keeping game logic fully decoupled from data.
example5_desc: Destroying entities inside a forEach corrupts iteration. The correct pattern is to collect IDs into an EM::deathSet during the loop and call destroyEntities afterwards — and destroyAll for scene resets.
example6_desc: forEach requires an entity to match all requested components and tags (AND). forEachAny visits if it matches at least one of the requested tags (OR). The example builds four entities with different component and tag combinations, then runs several queries to show exactly which entities each overload selects and why.
